title: Sea Turtle
summary: Sea Turtle, also tracked as Teal Kurma and Marbled Dust, is an intrusion set that public reporting since around 2017 describes as conducting state-aligned espionage through manipulation of the domain name system. The name service is the phone book of the internet: it turns a name people type into the network address of a server. Instead of only breaking into victim computers, operators linked to this cluster reportedly compromised registrars, registries and name servers, and modified records so that traffic for a target's own domains resolved to infrastructure the attackers controlled. That position supports credential interception through lookalike login pages, the collection of valid certificates to keep connections trusted, and the ability to read or alter traffic for mail and virtual private network services. Publicly reported victims were concentrated in government, media, telecommunications and energy organisations in the Middle East, North Africa and nearby regions, and researchers have noted the group often works from a small number of compromised hosting providers rather than from bespoke malware. Evidence is unusual and easy to miss in an endpoint-focused programme: certificate transparency entries for internal names, stale or unexpected authoritative name servers, successful authentication from addresses outside the approved ranges, and mail routing changes that users never reported. Attribution to a specific government is an assessment published with moderate confidence, and targeting has been reported as broadening over time. The common misunderstanding is that the domain name system is purely an infrastructure concern and therefore outside the security team's scope; in this cluster it is the primary intrusion surface, and it is often administered by people who are not security specialists.

beginner.definition: Sea Turtle is a name that researchers use for a group that spies on governments, media companies and telephone providers. Other reports call it Teal Kurma or Marbled Dust. Its special skill is taking control of the phone book of the internet. That system turns a website name into the correct server address. From there the group can quietly redirect traffic and read what users type.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security tools watch individual computers. This group attacks a shared service that everyone uses and trusts instead. When the phone book is altered, your staff reach the real login page address but see the attacker's copy. Passwords and mail can then be collected without any file ever landing on a laptop. It looks normal to users, so it can continue for a long time. Nobody asks why a certificate or a name server changed.
howItWorks: The attackers target the companies that manage domain names and their records.
They gain access to an account and change where a domain sends its traffic.
They request certificates for the real name, so the browser shows a trusted lock.
They build a copy of the login page and wait for staff to sign in there.
They use the stolen accounts to read mail and reach internal systems.
Defenders notice changed records, new certificates, or logins from odd places.
beginner.example: Imagine the postal service for your town is quietly bought by a stranger. Every letter still arrives at the right street, so nobody complains. But before delivery, each envelope is opened, copied and sealed again. The sender used the correct address and the receiver got the correct letter. Nothing looked wrong at either end. That is what a hijacked name service does. Checking who controls that service matters as much as checking the buildings.
takeaways: Protect your domain accounts with strong multi factor sign in, because they control your traffic.
Watch for unexpected certificate issuance and name server changes for your own domains.
Treat the domain name system as a security system, not only as an administrative detail.

objectives: Explain how domain name system record manipulation enables traffic redirection and credential theft.
Describe the role of certificates in making redirected traffic appear trustworthy to users.
Identify monitoring sources for domain and certificate changes, including transparency logs.
Explain why endpoint-only security programmes miss infrastructure-level intrusion activity.
Describe the reported targeting pattern of this cluster without overstating attribution confidence.
Recommend account protections for domain registrars, registries and name server providers.
